The system monitor service

monitord runs once on every MixOS host, as its own unprivileged user. It samples the system every second, keeps history, and answers questions about the host on the Bus. It only reads. The reasons are in the monitord decision.

Monitor, the task manager window, draws what monitord serves. Agents and scripts ask it directly.

Asking it

On the Bus, the service is monitord. Any node's monitord is reachable over the mesh as monitord.<node>.bus:

send monitord monitord.snapshot
print($reply.cpu.busy)

send monitord.alpha.bus monitord.processes sort=memory limit=5

Every verb is a query: it changes nothing. A refusal comes back with rc 10 and a body whose status says why: bad_request, not_found, unknown_verb, failed or busy.

VerbBodyReturns
monitord.status—Version, uptime, sample interval, whether the process sampler is running, and the history database's size and retention
monitord.snapshot—The system now (below)
monitord.processessort, reverse, limit, filter, user, tree, kernel_threadsThe process table
monitord.processpidOne process in full
monitord.series—The history series held: live and stored
monitord.historyseries, from or since, to, max_pointsPoints for each series

Unknown body fields are refused, so a typo is an error, not a silent default.

monitord.snapshot

Rates and percentages are over the last sample interval (interval_s). Sizes are bytes; rates are per second.

  • host, ts (Unix seconds), uptime_s, boot_time.
  • cpu: model, cores, and busy, user, system, iowait, steal in percent; per_core, a list of the same per CPU with mhz; context_switches_ps, forks_ps.
  • memory: total, available, used (total - available), free, cached, buffers, shared, dirty. swap: total, used, free.
  • load: one, five, fifteen, runnable, tasks.
  • pressure: for cpu, memory and io, the share of time tasks stalled (some, and full where the kernel reports it), each as avg10, avg60, avg300. Absent on kernels without PSI.
  • tasks: total, running, blocked.
  • disks: each whole disk with model, rotational, read_bps, write_bps, reads_ps, writes_ps and busy (percent of the interval with I/O in flight). Loop and RAM devices are left out.
  • filesystems: each real filesystem once per device, with mount, device, kind, total, used, available.
  • net: each interface but loopback, with state, physical, speed_mbps, rx_bps, tx_bps and the running totals.

A value monitord can't know is null, never zero.

monitord.processes

{"sort":"cpu", "limit":100, "filter":"firefox", "user":"alice", "tree":false}
  • sort is cpu (the default), memory, io, pid, name or user. Numbers sort largest first and names A to Z; reverse flips it.
  • limit defaults to 100; 0 means every row.
  • filter matches the name or command line, ignoring case.
  • tree puts parents before children, siblings in sort order, each row with its depth. A filter keeps a match's ancestors, so the tree still joins up.
  • The kernel's own threads are left out unless kernel_threads is true.

The reply has total (rows that matched), count (rows returned) and rows. Each row has pid, ppid, name, cmdline, user, uid, state, cpu, memory (resident), virtual_memory, threads, nice, priority, started_at, read_bps, write_bps, unit (the systemd service or scope) and kernel_thread.

cpu is a share of the whole machine, as Task Manager shows it: one busy core of eight is 12.5.

The process table is sampled only while someone reads it. A call keeps the sampler running for 30 seconds. The first call after a quiet spell takes two scans 0.3 s apart, so it answers in about a third of a second.

monitord runs unprivileged, so another user's I/O counters, open files and working directory are unreadable to it. Those fields are null.

monitord.process

{"pid": 1234} returns the table's fields plus exe, cwd, the whole cmdline, cpu_time_s, memory_peak, swap, read_bytes, write_bytes, open_files, voluntary_switches, involuntary_switches, cgroup and children.

monitord.history

{"series":["cpu.busy","net.*"], "since":3600, "max_points":600}
  • series is one name or a list. A name ending in * matches a prefix: cpu.core.* is every core.
  • Give from (Unix seconds) or since (seconds back from to); the default is the last ten minutes. to defaults to now.
  • Each point is [time, average, minimum, maximum]. Points are merged into buckets of step_s seconds so a series has at most max_points (default 600).
  • tier says where the points came from:
TierResolutionKeptSeries
liveevery sample10 minutesall, per core included
minute1 minute7 dayssystem-wide
hour1 hour1 yearsystem-wide

The series are cpu.busy, cpu.user, cpu.system, cpu.iowait, cpu.steal, mem.used, mem.available, mem.cached, swap.used, load.1, load.5, load.15, psi.<cpu|memory|io>.<some|full>, disk.<name>.<read|write|busy> and net.<name>.<rx|tx>, plus, in memory only, cpu.core.<n>.busy and cpu.core.<n>.mhz.

The summary topic

Every 5 seconds monitord publishes a small retained summary on monitord.summary: host, CPU busy and core count, memory, swap, load, total network and disk rates, the 10-second pressure figures and the task count. A mesh dashboard subscribes to it instead of polling every node.

The command line

The same binary works with no daemon running. It reads the kernel itself, so it answers on a node's console or over ssh either way:

monitord snapshot            the system now, sampled over half a second
monitord ps --sort memory    the process table (--tree, --user, --filter, --all)
monitord history cpu.busy --since 86400    stored history from the database
monitord signal 1234 TERM    send a signal, as you
monitord renice 1234 10      change a nice value, as you

--json prints what the matching verb returns. signal and renice run as the person who typed them, and the kernel decides whether they may. No Bus verb signals or renices anything: acting across users or nodes is hostd's job.

Running it

monitord.service runs /opt/mixos/bin/monitord serve as the user monitord, with no capabilities and a strict sandbox. The history database is /var/lib/monitord/history.db; it is a cache, and deleting it loses history and nothing else.

serve takes:

  • --interval-ms (default 1000);
  • --db PATH or --no-db;
  • --minute-days (default 7) and --hour-days (default 365);
  • --no-bus, to sample and record without joining the Bus.

When the broker is down, monitord keeps sampling and recording, and joins when it comes back.

Testing

cargo test -p monitord

The kernel readers take the text of each file, and the verb tests run against a fixture /proc and /sys tree, so no test needs a real host or a broker.
